I personally think that this is hilarious. YouTube's (and other large user content hosting companies) have ridiculously stupid copyright rules.

Anything that gets struck by a big company can get taken down, even if it's not true. There are a lot of copyright trolls (like patent trolls) out there.

Yep! If you follow esports at all, you'll know of all the trolls trying to mess stuff up in the scene.

DDoS attacks on pro games is super annoying, but something even more annoying is when VODs of games get taken down due to copyright. Some guy managed to claim copyright on the DRAFT SCREEN for Dota 2 which appears at the beginning of every game and looks almost identical every time.

YouTube needs to step up their game.
It's not just users. Private videos get yanked, too.

You have no idea how ridiculous the whole process is until you've gone through it.

So, like my profile says, I have a small youtube channel where I post LPs.

About 3 weeks ago I had a bot hit one of my videos. It was a video copyright claim against Minecraft. Which is beyond ridiculous. I know it was a bot because the video wasn't public yet. I disputed the claim, but the other "person" has 30 days to dispute it. They haven't responded. Meanwhile, I've got an episode of an ongoing series that isn't released because of it. It was a collaboration with another youtuber, so the other youtuber has released their video, which means the chances of me getting much traction on my version, when it comes out A MONTH LATER, is almost nil.

The big issue is that when a copyright claim is filed on a monetized video, even by a bot, the monetization is automatically set to the entity who filed the claim. So when a bot said that Boomvideotv actually owned part of the visual content on my video, if I did nothing, any money earned from that video automatically goes to Boomvideotv (which, btw, DOESN'T EVEN DO VIDEOS ANYMORE....they are LITERALLY a copyright troll) EVEN IF THE COPYRIGHT CLAIM IS FOUND TO BE FALSE, up until the time that it's found to be false. Most videos get the majority of their views when they first go up, so most of the money is earned early in the video's history. So it is in Boomvideotv's interest to file as many copyright claims as possible, even if they're false. If only 1 out of 100 people does nothing, they make money. And since it takes literally 0 input from them, there's no reason not to. In fact, if they DON'T respond, they're going to get a few more people that just say "screw it" and remove their dispute just to get the video out.

There are a couple ways to resolve this:

  1. Instead of automatically setting the monetization to the claimant, set it up so that until the issue is resolved the money is held in trust. This allows me, as a content creator, to publish my content knowing that I'm not infringing on anyone's copyright and I'm going to get my money without jeopardizing the amount of money I could earn on it.

  2. 30 days is a RIDICULOUS amount of time to respond to a claim put out by a bot. 48 hours is better, a week is absurd. There's no reason a copyright claimant needs 30 days to say "yes it is my content" after being identified by a bot.
